prose: SELL. The 12-month target price is USD 96.0, implying 72.5% downside from the current price of USD 348.52.

At USD 348.5201, Tesla's market cap is exactly USD 1.27 trillion and its enterprise value is USD 1.28 trillion. The reverse valuation reaches roughly USD 322 per share only if 2026 EBIT rises from the followed forecast of USD 5.7 billion to USD 22.6 billion and terminal EBIT margin reaches 43.2%. That profile resembles a scaled software platform more than Tesla's current mix. The followed model still forecasts negative FCFF in 2026 and 2027.

The evidence is not uniformly bearish. Tesla delivered 480,126 vehicles in Q2 2026, FSD Supervised reached 1.48m active users, and storage deployments reached 13.5 GWh. Cox Automotive reported that Tesla's US EV share rose to 55% in July. These are meaningful assets: a large installed base, proprietary driving data, a leading US fast-charging network and expanding storage capacity. They support a valuation above conventional automakers and mean the options should not be valued at zero.

The strongest case against SELL is that limited Texas driverless operations, Cybercab capacity and a 56% increase in FSD users may mark the start of a nonlinear platform shift. The robotaxi option could materially exceed the base valuation if Tesla secures broad driverless permissions, matches leading operators on crashes and interventions, and uses vehicle production as a low-cost fleet-supply channel. This does not change the call. California remains with-driver only, Nevada caps the fleet at ten vehicles, and the market already prices in much broader success.

The rating would improve if paid driverless fleets reach thousands of vehicles across several unrestricted jurisdictions, recurring FSD revenue exceeds the modelled path without eroding hardware margins, and Optimus publishes third-party uptime and task-cycle data. It would worsen if automotive gross margin remains near the lower reported Q2 range, storage price declines exceed cost reductions, or autonomy incidents delay permitting. The key investment indicators are regulatory fleet scale, paid software attachment and cost per deployed unit, not quarterly vehicle deliveries alone.

valuePools.name: Scaled unsupervised autonomy and robotaxi platform
deepDive: ### Size of the prize

A successful driverless platform would compete for household and enterprise transport spending, not only today's robotaxi revenue. ARK estimated a USD 10tn autonomous-mobility opportunity by 2030 and elsewhere put autonomous ride-hailing at USD 11tn–12tn. These are scenario estimates, not observed revenue. Published 2026 robotaxi-market estimates range from USD 1.18bn to USD 8.3bn, while another estimate was USD 2.63bn. The gap shows the difference between today's limited paid deployments and the spending that could shift if autonomous travel replaces private ownership and human-driven rides.

This report uses the USD 10tn long-run displaced-spend framework only for option legs, not current revenue. The household evidence suggests a high ceiling: US households spent USD 13,318 annually on transportation in 2024, AAA estimated USD 11,577 to own and operate a new car in 2025, and US vehicle-and-parts consumption reached USD 587bn in Q4 2025 on the cited quarterly basis. None of this spending automatically becomes platform revenue. Consumers may keep private cars, public transit remains available, and lower autonomous prices reduce revenue per mile even if mileage rises.
### What Tesla must capture

The base success leg assumes Tesla captures 1.25% of the USD 10tn displaced-spend opportunity by 2032, generating USD 125bn of revenue. At a 40% EBITDA margin, this produces USD 50bn of EBITDA. A 15.0x multiple gives USD 750bn of undiscounted success value. The upside leg assumes 2.5% share, USD 250bn revenue and a 40% margin, producing USD 100bn EBITDA at 18.0x. These are success-state endpoints, not blended forecasts. Probabilities, rather than conservative assumptions within each leg, drive expected value.

A 1.25% revenue share can arise through several operating combinations. At USD 0.50 of platform revenue per paid mile, USD 125bn requires 250bn annual miles. At 60,000 paid miles per active vehicle, this requires about 4.2m vehicle-equivalents; at 100,000 miles, about 2.5m. Tesla has not disclosed mature fleet utilization, so these are the report's scenario assumptions. Either outcome is far beyond current fleets and requires industrial-scale manufacturing, charging, cleaning, remote assistance, insurance and local operations.
### Unit economics

Industry estimates put scaled autonomous-fleet operating cost at USD 0.18–0.25 per mile, versus USD 0.75–0.84 for private-car ownership. ARK estimated a potential consumer price of USD 0.30–0.40 per mile by 2029. At a USD 0.40 price and USD 0.22 operating cost, vehicle-level contribution is USD 0.18 per mile before platform overhead, taxes and fleet financing. At 80,000 paid miles, that equals USD 14,400 annual contribution per vehicle. Low vehicle cost and high utilization are therefore essential.

The modelled 40% EBITDA margin is demanding but arithmetically consistent with a vertically integrated network. At USD 0.50 revenue per mile and USD 0.25 direct operating cost, gross contribution is 50%. Allowing ten percentage points for technology, customer support, local operations and corporate costs leaves 40% EBITDA. If direct cost reaches USD 0.35, the same price leaves only a 30% gross contribution and cannot support the success leg. A five-cent cost change across 250bn miles changes annual contribution by USD 12.5bn.
### Current commercial evidence

Tesla's robotaxi network reportedly reached nearly 2.5m cumulative paid miles by Q2 2026, including more than 380,000 unsupervised miles across six cities. Texas records showed an initial commercial deployment of 42 unsupervised Model Ys after Tesla self-certified SAE Level 4 compliance under Senate Bill 2807. Separate reports described unsupervised operations across seven US metros, including Miami, Orlando and Tampa. These reports show limited commercial activity but provide no independently audited revenue, utilization, remote-intervention frequency or city-by-city restrictions.

Cybercab entered production at Gigafactory Texas in Q2 2026, with installed annual capacity above 125,000 units. Steering-wheel-free vehicles were being tested on Austin roads by August. An Austin filing described a dedicated site with 80 wireless chargers. Manufacturing readiness appears ahead of broad regulatory permission. The US FMVSS exemption pathway for vehicles without traditional controls remains capped at 2,500 vehicles per manufacturer annually, and Tesla has not disclosed the status of its Cybercab exemption application.
### Competitors demonstrate demand but raise the evidence bar

- Waymo operated 3,871 active robotaxis and delivered 500,000 paid rides per week across ten US metropolitan areas by June 2026. Annualized revenue was estimated at USD 355m earlier in 2026.
- Baidu Apollo Go delivered approximately 1m fully driverless rides in Q2 2026 and had exceeded 23m cumulative public rides.
- Pony.ai and Uber announced plans for more than 2,000 robotaxis across five European cities, beginning in Zagreb.
- Tesla reported 2.5m cumulative paid miles, but did not disclose comparable fleet size, weekly rides or annualized revenue.

The sources identify Baidu as the leader on a composite autonomy index and Waymo as the global fleet-size and US leader. These claims are compatible: Baidu may lead a composite technology or deployment measure, while Waymo leads fleet size and US paid activity. For valuation, Waymo is the more relevant benchmark for US permissions and utilization, while Baidu shows large-scale driverless ride execution in China. Tesla must close the disclosure gap as well as the technology gap.
### Safety evidence

Tesla crossed 10bn cumulative FSD miles in May 2026, but most were supervised and cannot be treated as driverless miles. An Electrek analysis reported 14 Austin robotaxi crashes over 800,000 miles, or 17.5 crashes per million miles, approximately four times a cited urban human average. Definitions, reporting thresholds and fleet maturity can affect these comparisons. Still, the rate is adverse evidence and supports a low success probability until a larger, standardized dataset is available. NHTSA also required Tesla to submit information for a 58-incident FSD investigation.

NHTSA's recall query RQ24009 remains active on the effectiveness of the December 2023 Autopilot remedy. Nevada requires crashes, security incidents and system failures to be reported within five working days. California can issue traffic-violation notices directly to autonomous-vehicle companies under regulations effective July 2026. These rules increase transparency, but they can also lead to operating restrictions if safety performance disappoints.
### Jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction permission

Texas is the most positive jurisdiction. Tesla self-certified Level 4 status and deployed 42 unsupervised Model Ys under the state's framework. Self-certification does not mean a regulator independently validated safety, but it permits commercial learning and potential expansion if local operations remain compliant. Dallas and Houston restrictions, and remote-assistance practices, were not disclosed. The base probability therefore does not assume frictionless statewide scaling.

California is the clearest negative jurisdiction. As of 20 August 2026, the California DMV listed Tesla only for autonomous testing with a driver; Tesla lacked driverless testing and deployment permits. The CPUC said Tesla operated under a Charter-Party Carrier permit as a chauffeur service and had not applied to provide autonomous passenger service, paid or unpaid. California therefore contributes no approved public driverless scale to the base case despite its large technology and ride-hailing market.

Nevada granted an Autonomous Vehicle Network Company permit but capped the fleet at ten vehicles, limited speed to 45 mph and prohibited airport service. This allows operations, not economic scale. A ten-vehicle fleet cannot validate the multi-million-vehicle requirement derived above. The next measurable gate is a higher fleet cap, broader operating domains and compliant incident reporting.

Florida reports are more positive but less independently detailed. News sources described fully unsupervised launches in Miami, Orlando and Tampa, but local restrictions, independent crash rates and remote-intervention data were unavailable. The valuation gives these operations probability credit, not established economic value. The jurisdiction sequence is therefore Texas limited-commercial, Florida reported-commercial with incomplete detail, Nevada capped, and California not authorized.
### Probability and valuation

The base success leg receives a 25% probability. Supporting evidence includes the 42-vehicle Texas deployment, 2.5m cumulative paid miles, Cybercab capacity and the 10bn-mile supervised data asset. Offsetting evidence includes California's with-driver-only permit, no CPUC application, Nevada's ten-vehicle cap, the Austin crash-rate report and active NHTSA investigations. The upside leg receives 10%, leaving 65% for failure to reach either modelled scale.

The 65% failure remainder is the largest assumption because the critical condition is broad permission combined with safe, low-intervention economics, not demand. Failure includes small fleets, supervised-software sales or geofenced services that never reach millions of high-utilization vehicle-equivalents. This remains plausible while California is unavailable and Tesla has not published standardized intervention, utilization or cost-per-mile data. The technology may work while the option remains worth far less than a global platform.
### What would break the valuation

The option value would rise materially if Tesla secured California driverless testing and deployment permits, expanded Nevada beyond ten vehicles, disclosed thousands of paid vehicles and matched Waymo's safety performance on consistent definitions. Operating costs of USD 0.25 or less per mile, more than 60,000 paid miles per vehicle and limited remote intervention would support the 40% margin. Broad FMVSS clearance for steering-wheel-free Cybercab production would remove another bottleneck.

The option would approach zero if safety incidents lead to permit suspensions, Cybercab exemptions remain capped at 2,500 vehicles annually, or remote assistance and local operations prevent labor removal. It would also weaken if customers retain private vehicles and autonomous pricing proves too low to support fleet ownership. The key measures are paid rides, active driverless vehicles, intervention frequency, crash severity, cost per mile and jurisdictional fleet caps, not cumulative supervised miles alone.

valuePools.name: Optimus humanoid robotics
deepDive: ### Size of the prize

Humanoid robotics competes for labor spending in repetitive production, logistics and eventually services. ARK and Figure-related estimates put the long-run labor-displacement opportunity at USD 24tn, while another cited view reached USD 40tn. A nearer-term source estimated at least USD 1tn of annual accessible labor spend. These are economic ceilings, not current robot revenue. Published 2026 humanoid-market estimates are USD 6.24bn–10.9bn. Goldman Sachs forecast USD 38bn and 1.4m units by 2035, versus Barclays' USD 200bn estimate.

This report uses the USD 24tn labor-spend ceiling to construct success legs because the product substitutes for labor, but it assumes only a small Tesla share. The US had 23.726m workers in production and transportation/material-moving occupations in March 2025, while China's manufacturing sector employed more than 120m. These figures show the breadth of the market, but only some tasks will meet safety, dexterity, uptime and payback requirements. Humanoids compete task by task, not worker by worker.
### Required capture

The base success leg assumes Tesla captures 0.10% of the USD 24tn opportunity by 2035, equal to USD 24bn of revenue. At a 25% EBITDA margin, EBITDA is USD 6bn. A 15.0x multiple gives USD 90bn of undiscounted success value. The upside leg assumes 0.25% share, USD 60bn revenue, a 30% margin and USD 18bn EBITDA valued at 20.0x. These are success endpoints and are probability-weighted rather than diluted by midpoint operating assumptions.

At an average selling price of USD 40,000, USD 24bn of revenue requires 600,000 units annually. At USD 25,000, it requires 960,000. Tesla's public target of one million units per year in 2027 is broadly the scale required for the base success leg. However, the timing is not considered credible without production and customer evidence. The upside leg requires 1.5m units at USD 40,000 or 2.4m at USD 25,000, plus recurring service or software revenue if hardware prices fall.
### Customer economics

An estimated three-shift US manufacturing team costs USD 435,000 annually, including labor, benefits, overtime, training, turnover and rework. The source estimated fully loaded human manufacturing labor at USD 46.30 per hour. Humanoid running-cost estimates range from USD 2 per hour to USD 3 per hour, but may exclude or understate acquisition, financing, maintenance, supervision and downtime. The report treats these figures as eventual technical operating-cost targets, not current Tesla economics.

If a USD 40,000 robot delivers 6,000 productive hours annually for four years, straight-line acquisition cost is USD 1.67 per hour before maintenance and capital costs. Adding USD 3 of running cost, USD 2 of maintenance and USD 2 of supervision gives roughly USD 8.67 per productive hour. This can compete with USD 46.30 human cost only at high uptime and task productivity. At 50% productive utilization, effective cost roughly doubles. Uptime matters more than headline purchase price.
### Current capability evidence

Tesla has demonstrated internal tasks including sorting 4680 battery cells, moving parts between stations and visual quality inspection. Optimus Gen 3 reportedly has 50 hand actuators and 22 degrees of freedom, improving dexterity. Payload estimates range from 20kg to 45kg. Tesla said existing units were mainly learning and data-collection tools, rather than productive factory labor. No verified external customer trial, task cycle time, mean time between failures or human-intervention rate was available.

Reports differ on internal scale. One source estimated approximately 1,000 units deployed across Fremont and Austin by early 2026, while Omdia estimated fewer than 500 units built or shipped during 2025. The periods and definitions of deployed and built differ. The report therefore uses fewer than 1,000 as the evidence range rather than selecting the higher claim. Tesla and several competitors were each estimated at only about 1% of 2025 global shipments, with approximately 150 units in the shipment comparison.
### Production readiness

Tesla converted the former Fremont Model S/X line into an Optimus facility in a reported 46 days. Its Q2 2026 shareholder update targeted formal Gen 3 production for late July or August. Consumer sales were projected for the end of 2027, while longer-term Texas capacity ambitions reach 10m units annually. Factory conversion and start of production are relevant milestones, but installed capacity is not salable output. Yield, actuator supply, battery life, end-of-line testing and field service remain undisclosed.

Current build cost was estimated at USD 50,000–100,000 per unit. This exceeds Unitree G1's approximately USD 16,000 retail price and the assumed USD 40,000 base selling price. Cost must therefore fall materially before the base leg earns a hardware margin. At USD 60,000 cost and USD 40,000 price, every 100,000 units would lose USD 2bn before overhead. At USD 25,000 cost, the same volume would generate USD 1.5bn of gross profit. Cost and yield matter more than unit announcements.
### Competitive evidence

- Unitree led 2025 shipment estimates with 37.9% share and sells the G1 from approximately USD 16,000.
- AgiBot held an estimated 35.6% share, with 5,168 units sold in 2025.
- UBTech was separately identified as a revenue or broader-market leader with more than 14% share, reflecting a different market definition.
- Figure robots supported production of more than 30,000 BMW X3 vehicles during a ten-month pilot, and another report recorded over 200 autonomous sorting hours.
- Agility Robotics reported more than USD 300m of Digit v5 orders and a USD 2.5bn transaction valuation.

The Unitree and UBTech leadership claims reflect different metrics. Unitree appears to lead the cited shipment series, while UBTech leads a differently defined market estimate. Shipment leadership is more relevant for physical scale, while contracted orders and verified customer hours better measure commercial utility. Tesla has manufacturing resources and an internal proving ground, but Figure and Agility currently offer stronger named third-party evidence. The valuation probability reflects this gap.
### Safety and regulation

The EU AI Act classifies autonomous robotic systems as high risk, with conformity deadlines for stand-alone systems on 2 December 2027. Formal collaborative-workplace safety certifications for Optimus were not available. A humanoid working near people must manage pinch, impact, battery, cybersecurity and unintended-motion risks while maintaining predictable emergency-stop behavior. These approval requirements can delay external deployment after internal production begins.

Regulation is less fragmented than robotaxi permitting but remains material. Industrial customers can start with fenced or separated workflows, reducing risk and adding tasks as evidence builds. Consumer deployment is harder because homes are unstructured and include children, pets and fragile objects. The report assigns no near-term consumer economics and requires industrial reliability first.
### Probability and valuation

The base leg receives a 20% probability and the upside leg 5%, leaving 75% for failure to reach either modelled scale. Evidence supporting success includes factory conversion, targeted Gen 3 production, three demonstrated tasks, Tesla's manufacturing base and a large internal training environment. Evidence limiting probability includes the USD 50,000–100,000 current cost estimate, no verified external trial, no published uptime or intervention rate, and stronger third-party pilots from Figure and Agility.

The 75% failure remainder does not mean Optimus produces no robots. It means the product fails to reach at least USD 24bn of revenue and a 25% EBITDA margin by 2035. A technically capable but low-uptime robot, a product limited to a few internal tasks, or a system requiring frequent human teleoperation would all fall into that outcome. Demonstration success can coexist with low enterprise value.
### What would change the option

The probability would rise if Tesla disclosed thousands of units performing customer-valued tasks, more than 90% scheduled uptime, competitive cycle times and build costs below USD 40,000. Named external contracts, safety certification and service infrastructure matter more than choreographed demonstrations. A production ramp with gross-margin evidence would support the base leg. A million-unit claim without cost, yield and customer deployment would not.

The option would fall sharply if 2027 external sales slip, build cost remains above selling price, or competitor pilots show better reliability at lower prices. It would also weaken if task-specific automation captures the economic work without requiring a general humanoid form. The best investment measure is productive hours per robot per month at a disclosed intervention rate, followed by customer payback, not walking ability or factory-line capacity alone.

valuePools.name: Automotive hardware and leasing
deepDive: ### Size of the prize

Automotive hardware competes for spending on vehicle purchases and leases, not only a narrow EV category. Future Market Insights estimated the 2026 global car market at USD 2,789.2bn, while the IEA forecast 23m electric-car sales in 2026, nearly 30% of global vehicle sales. The broader spending pool matters because electrification changes the powertrain, not the customer's vehicle budget. Published 2026 estimates range from USD 147.57bn for vehicle leasing to USD 171.26bn for automobile rental and leasing. This report uses vehicle sales to frame hardware and treats leasing as a financing and residual-value overlay, rather than adding both markets mechanically.

The opportunity is also visible in displaced household spending. US vehicle ownership represented an estimated 17% of annual household expenses in 2026, and AAA estimated the annual cost of owning and operating a new car at USD 11,577 in 2025. This division captures only the purchase or lease component. Charging, insurance, service and software are valued elsewhere. This prevents an automotive multiple being applied to recurring software and service revenue. The division addresses trillions of dollars of spending, but its value depends on manufacturing margin per vehicle, not the size of the car market.
### From market size to Tesla's required capture

The intrinsic hardware valuation assumes Tesla remains a major global EV manufacturer without regaining its former global leadership. Statista reported 2025 Tesla BEV sales of 1.64m, down nearly 10%, versus BYD's 2.26m. An alternative industry series put Tesla at 1.79m, but both sources agree that BYD was larger. The report gives greater weight to 1.64m because it is consistent across the Statista comparison used for both companies, while recognizing definitional uncertainty. Against the IEA's 23m 2026 electric-car market, roughly 1.8m–2.0m annual deliveries would equal approximately 8%–9% of global EV units. That sustains scale but not software-like economics.

At the current control enterprise value, investors are not paying only for that unit share. Tesla's FY2025 revenue was USD 94.827bn, versus market enterprise value of USD 1,277.246bn. Even with substantial value assigned to software, energy and options, hardware must remain profitable and strategically useful because it supplies the installed base for FSD, service, charging and potentially robotaxi fleets. The base valuation assumes USD 6.0bn of sustainable hardware EBITDA at 10.0x, for USD 60.0bn of intrinsic EV. This is above conventional automaker valuations but recognizes direct distribution, the charging ecosystem and fleet-deployment value without double-counting autonomy.
### What the reported revenue pool contains

Tesla reported USD 69.526bn of total automotive revenue in FY2025, equal to the verified 73.3% reported-segment share. This reported segment differs from the business division because it includes vehicle hardware, leasing, regulatory credits and FSD revenue. The report therefore separates the division. Automotive sales excluding leasing and credits were USD 65.821bn, leasing was USD 1.712bn, and regulatory credits were USD 1.993bn. FSD revenue is assigned to supervised software. Regulatory credits remain in hardware economics because they arise from vehicle production, but receive no premium multiple.

The USD 68.026bn division-revenue estimate is not company-reported. It is derived from the automotive pool after removing the report's USD 1.5bn FSD estimate, leaving vehicle sales, leasing and credits in hardware. The figure reconciles exactly with the modelled division structure and does not create revenue outside the verified USD 94.827bn group total. FY2025 leasing revenue fell 6.29% to USD 1.712bn, and Q1 2026 leasing revenue was USD 381m. Leasing matters economically but is too small to alter the division's return profile, especially as Tesla does not disclose its financed fleet, residual-value performance or leasing margin.
### Volumes are improving, but price is decisive

Tesla produced 451,758 vehicles and delivered 480,126 in Q2 2026. Deliveries exceeded production by 28,368, reducing inventory pressure and showing that demand can respond to product, financing or pricing actions. However, Statista put average automotive revenue per delivery below USD 43,000 in Q2 2026, down from more than USD 50,000 in 2021. At 480,126 quarterly deliveries, each USD 1,000 change in realized revenue per delivery changes quarterly automotive revenue by roughly USD 480m before mix and lease-accounting effects. Cost reductions must therefore exceed price pressure.

The competitive picture varies by region. Cox Automotive reported Tesla at 55% of US EV sales in July 2026, well ahead of Chevrolet's 6% Q2 share. In China, Tesla's July NEV retail share fell to 2.87%, while BYD held 23.5%. Europe is also highly competitive: Volkswagen Group held 27% of the overall European car market in 2025. Tesla has a strong US franchise but cannot extrapolate that position globally. The base case assumes continued intense regional price competition.
### Product and capacity choices reduce risk but limit opportunity

Tesla ended Model S and Model X production in May 2026 and converted the Fremont line for Optimus. This removes low-volume premium models and concentrates the passenger portfolio around Model 3, Model Y and Cybertruck. Concentration can improve purchasing, factory complexity and working-capital efficiency. It also increases reliance on aging high-volume nameplates and raises the cost of a weak refresh cycle. With no confirmed Model 2 timing, the valuation does not assume an unannounced low-price model restores volume.

Commercial vehicles offer a separate source of growth. Tesla began volume production of Semi on a high-volume Nevada line in April 2026, and Einride reportedly ordered 500 trucks in August. These facts show production and customer interest, but not annual volume, realized price, warranty cost or margin. The base hardware EBITDA includes only a modest Semi contribution because one order does not prove fleet economics. Giga Shanghai's reported capacity of 950,000 vehicles annually remains important, but utilization for Shanghai, Berlin and Texas was not available and is not assumed.
### Margin evidence and the conflict in reported analysis

Two sources differ on Q2 2026 automotive gross margin excluding regulatory credits. Deep Research Global reported 14.6%, down from 16.3% in Q1. MLQ.ai and 36Kr cited 16.3% under alternative treatments excluding or normalizing one-time benefits. The report uses 14.6% as the conservative operating anchor and 16.3% as the upper end of the plausible range. The difference likely reflects classification and normalization choices. Neither figure is presented as a separately audited division margin.

At USD 68.026bn of modelled FY2025 revenue, a two-percentage-point gross-margin change equals approximately USD 1.36bn before operating-cost effects. The USD 6.0bn normalized EBITDA assumption implies an 8.8% division EBITDA margin. This is below Tesla's group 2026 forecast EBITDA margin of 15.7% because software and energy can have better economics. It still requires hardware cost reductions, credits and leasing earnings to cover substantial R&D and selling infrastructure. At the 14.6% gross-margin anchor, the division cannot absorb persistent price cuts and factory underutilization.
### Competitive comparison

- Tesla: 1.64m BEVs sold in 2025 in the consistently defined Statista series; Q2 2026 deliveries were 480,126.
- BYD: 2.26m BEVs sold in 2025 and approximately 557,090 in Q2 2026, showing greater global unit scale.
- Volkswagen Group: 27% of the overall European car market in 2025, supported by multiple brands and broad distribution.
- Chevrolet: 6% of US EV sales in Q2 2026 versus Tesla's leading US position.
- Ayvens and Arval: leasing fleets of approximately 3.1m and 1.9m vehicles respectively, far larger than any disclosed Tesla leasing fleet.

The comparison shows why Tesla merits neither a pure legacy-auto multiple nor an unrestricted technology multiple. BYD is the key volume benchmark. Volkswagen shows the manufacturing and distribution scale required in Europe, while Chevrolet demonstrates Tesla's wide US lead. Specialist lessors show that Tesla leasing is not independently scaled. Hardware also has capital intensity that software lacks. The followed model forecasts group capex of USD 19.354bn in 2026 and USD 21.690bn in 2027, limiting the cash value of accounting earnings during this investment phase.
### Valuation, assumption and break point

The division is valued at USD 60.0bn of intrinsic EV, using USD 6.0bn of normalized EBITDA and a 10.0x multiple. The multiple is close to Toyota's 2026 11.8x EV/EBITDA and above GM's 6.0x and Volkswagen's 4.9x, reflecting Tesla's direct model, EV scale and ecosystem. It remains below the group's 101.83x normalized historical EV/EBITDA average because that premium includes options valued separately here. An 8.0x multiple would reduce division EV by USD 12bn, while 12.0x would add USD 12bn.

Value depends on manufacturing-cost reductions at least matching realized-price pressure, annual deliveries staying near or above the 2025 scale, and core factories avoiding prolonged underutilization. The case breaks if average revenue per delivery keeps falling while ex-credit gross margin remains near 14.6%, or if China and Europe share losses require sustained incentives. A stable 18%–20% ex-credit automotive gross margin, rising revenue per delivery and profitable Semi scaling would support EBITDA above USD 6.0bn. The key monitor is gross profit per delivery: unit growth can still destroy economic value.

valuePools.name: Supervised driver-assistance software
deepDive: ### Size of the prize

Supervised driver-assistance software competes first for what drivers will pay for convenience and safety, not for the full transport budget a driverless service could replace. Published market definitions differ by more than an order of magnitude. Global Market Insights estimated the 2026 autonomous-driving software market at USD 3bn, while Market Research Future estimated autonomous-car software at USD 33.18bn in 2025. Broader definitions are larger: Global Market Insights put the 2025 self-driving-car market, including hardware and supervised ADAS, at USD 202.4bn, versus Custom Market Insights' USD 36.5bn ADAS estimate. This report uses the software opportunity, not the mobility spending reserved for the unsupervised robotaxi option.

This difference defines what can be valued today. A supervised system still needs a human driver, so it does not replace driver labor, private-car ownership or the USD 13,318 annual US household transportation expenditure reported by the Bureau of Labor Statistics for 2024. Its revenue pool is the price customers pay for software functions and subscriptions. The valuation therefore starts with users multiplied by annual revenue per user, using deferred-revenue recognition as a cross-check. It does not include hypothetical autonomous ride revenue in supervised software.
### Tesla's required capture

Tesla reported 1.48m active FSD Supervised users at Q2 2026, up 56% year over year. More than 55% of new North American deliveries included an FSD subscription at purchase. This is a strong flow indicator but may exceed the attach rate across the global installed fleet. At an estimated USD 65m monthly subscription run-rate in July, annualized subscription revenue would be USD 780m. Dividing this by 1.48m active users implies approximately USD 527 per active user per year, or USD 44 per month. This suggests the global user figure includes trials, bundled access, regional pricing or non-paying active users.

The report therefore does not apply headline list pricing to all users. The USD 1.5bn FY2025 division-revenue estimate combines USD 956m of disclosed deferred FSD revenue recognized during the year with an assumed USD 544m of current-period subscriptions and software purchases not separately reported. This is a modelled estimate, not reported revenue, and remains within the range implied by the July 2026 run-rate. Exact FY2025 cash sales and subscriber mix are unavailable. The estimate is bounded by recognized deferred revenue at the low end and the later subscription run-rate at the high end.
### Revenue architecture and economic leverage

Tesla's automotive deferred-revenue balance was USD 3.867bn at December 2025 and included FSD features and internet connectivity. The balance is not entirely FSD and cannot be treated as future FSD revenue without adjustment. It nevertheless shows that cash receipts can precede full feature recognition, creating a revenue tail as functionality is delivered. The disclosed USD 956m recognized from deferred FSD revenue in FY2025 equals about 64% of the report's modelled division revenue. Recognition policy and feature delivery therefore matter to annual growth.

The high-margin case relies on software being reused across an installed fleet whose hardware costs sit largely in automotive. Tesla does not disclose FSD-only gross margin, and the report does not claim a reported margin. The bridge assumes USD 2.5bn of sustainable EBITDA at revenue above the FY2025 estimate. Paid users, revenue per paying user and recognition of the deferred balance must therefore expand. A 70%–80% incremental margin is a plausible model assumption for software delivered to compatible vehicles, but customer incentives, compute, data labeling, support, regulatory localization and included hardware rule out a 100% margin.
### Product evidence and the data advantage

Cumulative FSD Supervised mileage reached 8.4bn miles by February 2026 and passed 10bn by May. This data accumulation matters because rare driving events require exposure to many edge cases. Tesla's consumer fleet can collect geographically diverse examples without an equivalent dedicated test fleet. However, cumulative miles are an input, not a safety outcome. They do not show miles between safety-critical interventions, crash severity, cross-country transferability or performance in an unsupervised operating domain.

A November 2025 third-party test series reported an average 1,454 miles between critical disengagements for FSD v14. The source was a Reddit-linked real-world dataset, rather than a regulator or standardized audit, so it is treated as directional. The supervised product can create customer value before it reaches driverless reliability. This distinction protects current software revenue from an all-or-nothing autonomy case while preventing supervised miles from being presented as proof of unsupervised readiness.
### Geographic authorization

Tesla said at CVPR 2026 that FSD Supervised was approved or available in ten countries: the United States, Canada, Mexico, China, South Korea, Australia, New Zealand, the Netherlands, Lithuania and Estonia. Another June source counted eleven jurisdictions by including Denmark, showing the difference between country availability, partial authorization and mutual recognition. Netherlands approval in August 2026 was described as the first such European Union approval. Denmark, Belgium, Lithuania and Estonia had recognized Dutch type approval through EU mechanisms. The report uses Tesla's ten-country count and treats the wider European rollout as developing, not fully equivalent deployment.

- Approved or available: US, Canada, Mexico, South Korea, Australia and New Zealand, with China described as partial in the source set.
- European foothold: Netherlands approval in August 2026; Lithuania and Estonia included in Tesla's June availability list.
- Recognition path: Denmark and Belgium reportedly recognized the Dutch approval framework, but exact commercial feature availability and local restrictions were not disclosed.
- Next gate: sustained European availability with disclosed paid-user conversion, not approval headlines alone.

Regulation matters differently for supervised software than for robotaxi. Supervised approval can expand software revenue while the driver remains legally responsible, making it less demanding than commercial driverless authorization. Tesla can therefore monetize localization work even if robotaxi approval takes years. It also faces regional pricing and liability complexity. Value depends on paid attachment after initial trials, not the number of countries shown on an availability map.
### Competition and pricing

Mobileye shipped 10m EyeQ systems in H1 2026 and reported a USD 50.8 average system price in Q4 2025. Its more advanced SuperVision package was estimated at USD 150–200 per unit. This remains well below recurring consumer FSD revenue because Mobileye mainly sells components and integrated systems to automakers. Huawei had installed Qiankun ADS in 1.4m vehicles by the end of 2025 and raised the subsidized buyout price to CNY 15,000 in July 2026. XPeng reported 85% penetration for XNGP urban smart driving among active users in June 2025, showing that high feature usage need not require a separately priced Tesla-style subscription.

These competitors define Tesla's monetization challenge. Tesla seeks more revenue per equipped vehicle than a component supplier, which requires consumers to see sustained differentiated utility and improvement. Huawei shows a premium buyout alternative, while XPeng shows how bundling can compete. The installed base can grow while pricing falls if advanced assistance becomes standard equipment. The report therefore assumes recurring revenue per active user below headline annual subscription pricing and tests value against attach rate rather than total compatible vehicles.
### Why the attach rate is decisive

A 55% new-delivery attach rate in North America is encouraging but cannot be applied globally. If Tesla delivers 2m vehicles annually and sustains a 30% global paid attach rate, it adds 600,000 users per year before churn. At USD 600 annual revenue per paying user, that cohort generates USD 360m of annualized revenue. At 50% attachment, it generates USD 600m. The USD 240m difference could be worth several billion dollars under a software multiple. Paid global attachment matters more than one quarter's deliveries.

The installed fleet provides a second upgrade channel, but older vehicles may need hardware changes and customers who declined the feature at purchase may be less willing to pay later. A subscription-only model lowers the upfront barrier but can increase churn. The base case assumes active users keep growing while paid users remain below total active users, consistent with the USD 527 implied annual run-rate per active user. If all 1.48m users paid a materially higher subscription price, reported revenue would be visibly above the available run-rate estimate.
### Valuation, assumption and break point

The division is valued at USD 50.0bn of intrinsic EV, using USD 2.5bn of normalized EBITDA at 20.0x. The multiple is below valuations requiring durable 20%–30% growth, but above Alphabet's 17.4x and Uber's 14.0x 2026 EV/EBITDA because the revenue can scale across Tesla's installed fleet. This is not current reported EBITDA. It is a modelled sustainable contribution after further user growth. A 16.0x multiple would reduce EV by USD 10bn, while 24.0x would add USD 10bn.

The case assumes active users convert to recurring paying users at a sustainable global attach rate, with annual revenue per paying user sufficient to cover localization and compute costs. It breaks if attachment is trial-driven, competitors bundle comparable systems, or regulators restrict functions after safety events. It strengthens if Tesla reports subscription revenue at or above the USD 780m annualized July run-rate, maintains more than 50% North American paid attachment and expands European paid availability. The most useful quarterly disclosures are paying subscribers, churn and recognized software revenue. Until then, valuation should remain bounded rather than extrapolated from active users alone.

valuePools.name: Energy storage
deepDive: ### Size of the prize

Energy storage competes for spending on grid capacity, peak generation, balancing, resilience and behind-the-meter backup, not only for a labelled battery-system market. A complete dollar estimate for displaced gas-peaker spending was unavailable, so the report uses deployment as its anchor. BloombergNEF reported 112 GW of non-pumped-hydro storage additions in 2025, up 48%, and forecast 158 GW in 2026. Storage was also reported to have fallen below gas-peaker costs in some applications by mid-2026, expanding its role from renewable integration to capacity substitution.

The physical market is expanding faster than most Tesla businesses, but value per unit is declining. BloombergNEF put 2025 turnkey stationary-storage cost at approximately USD 117/kWh. It would be wrong to multiply this by 112 GW because GW measures power and GWh measures energy; a duration assumption is required. A four-hour system contains four times the energy of a one-hour system. The valuation therefore uses Tesla's disclosed GWh deployments and revenue pool instead of constructing a global dollar TAM from incompatible units. The key question is whether deployment growth can exceed price declines.
### Required share and division revenue

Tesla deployed 46.7 GWh in FY2025, up 49%, and Benchmark Mineral Intelligence ranked it second among global BESS integrators with approximately 10% share. BYD shipped more than 60 GWh and held 13%, while Sungrow held 9%. Tesla is scaled but not dominant. Chinese integrators held eight of the top ten positions and 76% share, according to Wood Mackenzie. The base case assumes Tesla retains a high-single-digit to low-double-digit global integration share rather than restoring clear leadership.

Tesla reported USD 12.771bn of FY2025 energy generation and storage revenue, including USD 12.270bn of sales and USD 501m of leasing. Storage revenue is not separately disclosed. The report models USD 12.0bn for storage and USD 771m for solar, based on deployment growth, the segment's strategic focus and the lack of solar deployment disclosure after 2023. This split is an estimate, not Tesla guidance. It reconciles exactly to the verified segment pool and avoids assigning all energy revenue to storage.
### Deployment and implied revenue per GWh

Dividing modelled FY2025 storage revenue of USD 12.0bn by 46.7 GWh gives approximately USD 257m per deployed GWh, or USD 257/kWh of revenue. This exceeds the USD 117/kWh global turnkey cost benchmark because Tesla revenue may include integration, power electronics, software, installation, service and product mix. The benchmark measures system-level cost, not seller revenue. The difference is not gross profit. It shows that project scope and the Powerwall versus Megapack mix can materially change implied revenue per GWh.

Q2 2026 deployments reached 13.5 GWh, up 53% sequentially, while energy generation and storage revenue was USD 3.14bn, up 13% year over year. Dividing all quarterly segment revenue by storage deployments gives about USD 233/kWh, but includes solar and leasing and is therefore only an upper-bound measure. More importantly, deployment growth exceeded revenue growth. This is consistent with lower value per GWh, changing mix or revenue-recognition timing. Gross profit per GWh, not deployment alone, drives valuation.
### Margin quality and the warranty charge

Energy gross margin fell to 20.4% in Q2 2026 from 39.5% in Q1. Tesla attributed part of the decline to a USD 240m warranty charge related to vendor cell issues. Adding back this charge would improve normalized economics, but would not show that Q1 margin is sustainable because mix and project timing also matter. The report uses 20.4% as the observed downside margin and the high-20s as a normalized planning range, rather than carrying forward 39.5%.

At USD 3.14bn of quarterly segment revenue, the 19.1-percentage-point fall from Q1 to Q2 represents roughly USD 600m of gross profit, although revenue and mix changes make this directional. The USD 240m warranty charge explains about 7.6 percentage points of Q2 revenue. Even after adjustment, a substantial gap remains versus the prior quarter. This supports a 12.5x EBITDA multiple, rather than a premium software multiple, despite strong growth.
### Capacity supports growth but creates utilization risk

Tesla's Lathrop Megafactory reportedly has 40 GWh of annual capacity, and Shanghai adds another 40 GWh. A planned Houston/Brookshire facility targets 50 GWh once ramped, with Megapack 3 production starting in late 2026. Existing 80 GWh of capacity compares with 46.7 GWh deployed in 2025, implying approximately 58% deployment-to-nameplate capacity if both factories had been available and fully ramped throughout the year. They were not necessarily at steady state. This is a report-derived guide, not a reported utilization rate.

If 130 GWh of nominal capacity becomes available and deployments reach 90 GWh, utilization would be about 69%. At USD 200/kWh of revenue, that volume would imply USD 18bn of revenue; at USD 150/kWh, it would imply USD 13.5bn. The USD 4.5bn difference shows the sensitivity to price. Capacity creates value only if backlog, cell supply and installation execution keep factories full without sacrificing price or warranty quality.
### Competition by segment

- Utility-scale integration: BYD shipped more than 60 GWh in 2025 and held 13% share, Tesla deployed 46.7 GWh and held 10%, and Sungrow held 9%.
- Global supply structure: Chinese integrators held eight of the top ten positions and 76% of the 2025 market, increasing price competition.
- US residential storage: estimates differ, with Powerwall 3 at approximately 35% by mid-2025 and 63% in Q1 2026.
- Regional challenge: Sigenergy reached 25% in Australia in early 2026, while Huawei benefited from a 35% solar-inverter position in Ireland.

The Powerwall share estimates should be treated as a range. Mordor Intelligence's 35% estimate referred to mid-2025, while Clean Energy Reviews' 63% referred to early 2026 and may reflect a different channel or product scope. A real share gain is possible, but the evidence does not show Tesla controlled 63% of all US residential storage. The valuation assumes strong US residential positioning without extending it globally, where inverter channels and local installers can favor Huawei, Sungrow or Sigenergy.
### Unit economics

The base intrinsic valuation assumes USD 4.0bn of normalized EBITDA. Against USD 12.0bn of modelled FY2025 storage revenue, this implies a 33% margin and is not a current-year forecast. It requires revenue growth toward approximately USD 18bn–20bn, gross margin in the high-20s or better, warranty normalization and operating leverage from dedicated factories. At USD 18bn of revenue and a 22% EBITDA margin, EBITDA would be about USD 4.0bn. These assumptions are demanding but achievable if deployments grow while revenue per GWh declines gradually rather than collapsing.

A downside case assumes 70 GWh at USD 150/kWh, producing USD 10.5bn of revenue, a 15% EBITDA margin and USD 1.6bn of EBITDA. An upside case assumes 100 GWh at USD 220/kWh, producing USD 22bn of revenue, a 24% margin and USD 5.3bn of EBITDA. The base lies between these outcomes. This range matters because combining current deployment growth with past pricing would overstate value, while using falling battery costs without integration revenue would understate it.
### Valuation and break point

The division is valued at USD 50.0bn of intrinsic EV, using USD 4.0bn of normalized EBITDA and 12.5x. The multiple is below Enphase's 13.7x 2026 EV/EBITDA and close to Toyota's 11.8x despite higher growth, reflecting project cyclicality, warranty risk and Chinese competition. Fluence's negative forecast EBITDA makes its multiple unusable, but its 0.7x 2026 EV/Sales shows how the market values unprofitable storage integrators. A 10.0x multiple would reduce value by USD 10bn, while 15.0x would add USD 10bn.

Value depends on deployment growth exceeding price erosion, gross margin normalizing after the vendor-cell charge, and capacity filling without excessive working capital. It breaks if revenue per GWh falls faster than manufacturing and procurement costs, warranties recur, or Chinese integrators push Tesla toward commodity returns. It strengthens if quarterly deployments remain above 13 GWh, normalized energy gross margin exceeds 25%, and new factories show visible backlog. The key monitor is revenue and gross profit per deployed GWh, alongside warranty charges and factory-loading evidence.

valuePools.name: Ownership services, charging and insurance
deepDive: ### Recurring spend opportunity

This division competes for recurring spending after vehicle purchase: electricity, maintenance, parts, used vehicles and insurance. The 2026 EV-charging-station market was estimated at USD 22.93bn, while switching from combustion vehicles to EVs was estimated to save USD 1,545 of fuel annually. Tesla does not capture all displaced fuel spending. However, its approximately 38,000 US Supercharger ports represented 52% of the 73,000 public DC fast-charge ports operating in June 2026. The network generates revenue and supports vehicle demand.

FY2025 services and other revenue was USD 12.530bn, but Tesla does not separately disclose GAAP revenue for Supercharging, used vehicles, service, parts and insurance. Insurance direct premiums written were USD 1.37bn, up 40.7%, but premiums written are not the same as recognized revenue. The report therefore values the combined division rather than inventing individual revenue lines. The recurring opportunity scales with vehicles in operation, charging utilization and third-party network access.
### Insurance increases monetization but adds balance-sheet risk

Tesla directly underwrote 75.9% of premiums in 2025, up from 32.6%, taking more claims risk onto its own carriers. The carriers reported a USD 17m underwriting gain in Q1 2026 after a reserving-methodology change, their first profitable quarter in the register. This is encouraging but does not establish a through-cycle margin. California's Department of Insurance also acted on claims handling and threatened certificate suspension. Service quality and reserving governance are therefore valuation issues, not back-office details.
### Competition and valuation

Tesla's US charging lead is much stronger than its international position. Electrify America and ChargePoint were estimated at 7.9% and 6.9%, respectively, in a Q2 2026 comparison. Tesla operated 2,026 rapid or ultra-rapid chargers in the UK at December 2025 and ranked behind InstaVolt. Intrinsic value is USD 25.0bn, based on USD 2.5bn of normalized EBITDA and 10.0x. The case breaks if service costs rise faster than fleet revenue, low utilization dilutes charging returns, or insurance losses and regulatory sanctions absorb cross-sell benefits.

valuePools.name: Solar generation
deepDive: ### Opportunity and current position

Solar competes for electricity spending displaced by self-generation. Estimates of the 2025 global electricity-retailing market range from USD 3.04tn to USD 3.25tn, while the narrower solar-PV panel market was estimated at USD 198.91bn. The report uses the product and installation opportunity because Tesla does not capture the customer's entire displaced utility bill. Tesla last disclosed 223 MW of deployments in 2023 and has not separately disclosed deployments since. This suggests solar is no longer a primary growth disclosure.

The report models USD 771m of FY2025 solar revenue as the residual of the USD 12.771bn verified energy segment after assigning USD 12.0bn to storage. This is not a reported split. Tesla's US residential-solar share was estimated at 4.8% in 2023, below Sunrun's 12.7% 2025 share and Freedom Forever's 6.1% before its April 2026 bankruptcy. The market remains fragmented and financially difficult. Competitor distress may release demand, but it also signals weak installation economics.
### Economics, valuation and failure condition

Solar panels are globally commoditized. JinkoSolar and LONGi tied for the leading shipment position in H1 2026, and the top ten accounted for 59% of shipments. Tesla must therefore differentiate through customer acquisition, installation, financing and Powerwall integration, rather than module manufacturing. The intrinsic valuation assumes USD 200m of eventual EBITDA at 20.0x, or USD 4.0bn EV. The high multiple applies to a small normalized profit base and reflects bundled home-energy potential, not strong current solar economics.

Solar ceases to be a meaningful stand-alone contributor if deployments continue to decline or remain undisclosed because they are immaterial. It could outperform if Tesla reports renewed MW growth, proves profitable Powerwall-plus-solar bundles and uses its vehicle customer base to reduce acquisition costs. Until then, solar is treated as a modest feeder for storage rather than a core enterprise-value driver.

executiveMap: Most of Tesla's current market value sits in two pre-revenue options. Scaled unsupervised autonomy represents 55% of control EV and requires broad permission, cost below approximately USD 0.25 per mile, and millions of high-utilization vehicle-equivalents. Optimus represents 18% and requires productive uptime, build cost below commercial price, and third-party task validation. These two divisions explain more of the share price than reported automotive or energy revenue.

The current earnings base is automotive hardware, modelled at USD 68.026bn FY2025 revenue; supervised software at USD 1.5bn; storage at USD 12.0bn; solar at USD 771m; and ownership services at USD 12.530bn. The key measures are gross profit per delivery, paid FSD attach rate, gross profit per deployed GWh, renewed MW deployment and recurring revenue per vehicle in operation.

The followed model forecasts group revenue rising from USD 105.880bn in 2026 to USD 144.000bn in 2028. FCFF remains negative through 2027 before turning positive in 2028. Tesla's net cash can fund investment in the options, but this cash profile does not support the current valuation without much higher later margins. The analysis separates strategically useful assets from the price investors currently pay for them.
coreAnalysis.analyticalAnchor: The investment case is a probability question: current businesses support a substantial company, but the share price requires broad autonomy and robotics success before the evidence passes the relevant gates.
crossPoolBridge: Automotive hardware provides the installed base for FSD, service, insurance and charging. Lower vehicle prices can expand the addressable software and service base, but they destroy value if lost hardware gross profit exceeds lifetime recurring revenue.

Storage and services can fund autonomy and robotics investment, although both require capital and working capital. Solar can reduce Powerwall acquisition costs through bundling, while Supercharging can serve private vehicles and robotaxi depots.

Robotaxi could cannibalize private Tesla purchases if mobility becomes cheaper than ownership. Optimus also competes for factory capital and took over the former Model S/X line. The SOTP values each division separately but does not assume every strategic option succeeds without trade-offs.
coreAnalysis.bridgeMechanics: Profit engines are valued on normalized EBITDA using division-appropriate multiples. Pre-revenue options are valued only through explicit assumptions for future revenue share, margin, multiple, probability and discounting. The unassigned probability represents failure.
valuationRealityCheck: Tesla trades at 76.86x 2026 EV/EBITDA, 225.18x EV/EBIT and 267.91x P/E. The 14-peer medians are 13.7x, 19.7x and 11.2x, respectively. Mix and optionality support a premium, but only if future earnings move toward software economics.

Tesla's own normalized historical averages are also high: 101.83x EV/EBITDA and 112.06x P/E. Historical prices repeatedly capitalized future businesses, making these averages unsuitable for valuing hardware or storage on a stand-alone basis.

The reverse valuation requires 2026 EBIT of USD 22.567bn, versus the followed USD 5.672bn. It raises terminal EBIT margin to 43.2% and produces USD 7.679bn of 2026 FCFF, instead of the followed negative USD 4.454bn.

The intrinsic SOTP still assigns significant value to autonomy and Optimus. The difference is timing and probability. Limited Texas activity, California's with-driver-only status, Nevada's cap and the absence of Optimus uptime evidence do not justify treating global scale as the base outcome.
scenarios: The bear case assumes persistent hardware price pressure, energy margin normalizing near the Q2 level, and zero option value because permission or commercial reliability fails. Revenue reaches USD 120bn, but a 10% EBITDA margin and a manufacturing-weighted multiple provide little support for the current share price.

The base case takes the revenue-producing divisions toward USD 155bn of revenue and USD 27.9bn EBITDA. It assigns probability-weighted value to robotaxi and Optimus, treating both as real options but not as the most likely stand-alone outcomes.

The bull case assumes driverless fleet expansion across major jurisdictions, higher FSD attachment, full storage factories and meaningful Optimus sales. Revenue reaches USD 250bn and EBITDA USD 62.5bn. As success generates cash, the scenario does not mechanically retain base-case net debt.

The path between cases is observable. Autonomous fleet caps and paid rides, FSD paying users, storage gross profit per GWh, automotive gross profit per delivery, and Optimus productive uptime determine which scenario becomes credible.
coreAnalysis.bottomLine: Tesla owns valuable physical and data assets, but the current USD 1.28 trillion enterprise value assigns most value to businesses whose permission, reliability and economics remain unproven at scale. The USD 115.8 target already includes substantial robotaxi and Optimus option value. Investors may disagree with the target but should monitor paid driverless scale, gross profit per delivery, software attachment, storage value per GWh and robot uptime when sizing positions.

scenarioValuation.keyConditions: The bear case assumes no option value and continued manufacturing pressure. Higher cash generation improves the equity bridge rather than retaining base net debt unchanged. valuation.methodRationale:
SOTP is primary because manufacturing, software, energy, services and pre-revenue options have different economics. Profit engines use normalized EBITDA multiples within named peer brackets; robotaxi and Optimus use explicit success-state revenue, margin, multiple and probability, discounted from the scale year. Core multiples are deliberately below Tesla's option-laden history. The target gives 100% weight to SOTP, while the sensitivity isolates the effect of core EBITDA and its blended multiple.

What the market is pricing.

The USD 1,277.246bn market EV exceeds the approximately USD 189bn undiscounted core-business EV by USD 1,088bn. Using the report's discounted option success values, the quote requires roughly three to four times the base probability-weighted autonomy and robotics value—economically similar to treating broad robotaxi success as more likely than failure while also assigning substantial Optimus success.

The market assumes Broad robotaxi scale is effectively the central outcome. We assign a different reading: Base probability is 35% across two success legs; California with-driver-only status and Nevada's ten-vehicle cap keep failure the largest outcome. (California DMV, CPUC and Nevada Transportation Authority, March–August 2026)

The market assumes Tesla can rapidly approach software-platform margins. We assign a different reading: The followed 2026 EBIT margin is 5.4%; the reverse model requires 21.3% immediately and 43.2% terminally, so the market assumes an earnings-mix transition not yet visible. (Valuatum followed model and reverse valuation, 2026)

The market assumes Optimus manufacturing announcements establish commercial scale. We assign a different reading: The report assigns only 25% total probability to modeled success because no external trial, uptime, cycle-time or intervention data were verified. (Tesla Q4 2025 call; Figure/BMW and Agility evidence, June–August 2026)

Two enterprise values, two questions. The division pages allocate today's market enterprise value across the divisions; the target-price bridge states what each is worth on this report's own estimates. For Scaled unsupervised autonomy and robotaxi platform the two readings are 702.5 billion allocated and 209.2 billion warranted.
